en.title: Dock Office — Time Cards, Night Zero
en.text: The rack by the dock-office window holds the shift's time cards, and the clock stamp on every one of them reads 22:00 — the hour the outage was scheduled for one hour and then was not scheduled for anything ever again. Nobody stamped out. The cards are still in the rack because the men are still on the floor, the night foreman's margin note says so in a hand that got worse as it went: "Machines took the 22:00 cycle on their own. I am not initialing that. City Power pinned the outage notice to the board and the board is the only thing in this plant that stopped when it was told." Pinned under the cards, the notice itself, and a strike leaflet three months older: the men demanded the night shift be shut down while there were still men to demand things. Nobody signed the reply. The reply was the schedule unchanged.

notes.location_hint: Time-card rack in the dock office window (z_loading_dock)

en.title: Photo: Workshop B, 23:15
en.text: A plant-safety photograph, timestamped 23:15 — the exact minute the shift log stopped being a log and started being testimony. Workshop B lit by a single overhead that should not have been lit: every feeder in the city was dark by then, and this one lamp is burning at full warm throw over a bench where nothing is plugged in. In the foreground, the peening press mid-stroke. No operator's hands. The print is blurry the way photographs are when the photographer's hands are shaking, and on the back, one line: "This is the third frame like this. I did not take the first two. The camera was in the locker."

notes.location_hint: Taped inside the peening-press guard rail (z_factory_floor)

en.title: Recorder: Grid Crew Log 19 — Factory Stores
en.text: "Stores check, the factory this time. Marat's count again: fuses by the crate in the yard bins, transistor stock behind the switchgear door — that one's locked and the key will be in the foreman's office, same as the depot, same as everywhere, they all lock the solid state and lose the key at a desk. Gears and billet stock enough to roof a house. But listen — the line in Workshop B is running. Slow, no load on it, and it is sorting lamp fittings. Brass shells, the kind we found on the suburbs bench. It sorts them onto a pallet with no order number and no destination street, and when I put my hand on the conveyor bed it is warm like the transformer was warm. We are taking what we came for and we are not standing between that line and its pallet. Recorder's note: the pallet was fuller on our way out than our way in."

notes.location_hint: Recorder left on the Workshop B bench, beside the line (z_workshop_b)

en.title: Shipping Ledger — Orders 14,207 and 14,208
en.text: The works ledger, kept since the plant opened. The grid went up district by district off this dock — every lamp housing, every bracket, the whole city's iron stamped and shipped row by row, and the last of the great orders is 14,207: two hundred and nineteen lamp fittings, suburbs, received in full by a lamplighter who signed in a hand like a ruled line and was still signing forty years later. Then the gap. Decades of small work. And the final entry, dated weeks after the lights failed, in the day foreman's hand: order 14,208 — inbound, not outbound. DISMANTLE. TRANSFORMERS TO THE CENTER. The old lamplighter stood at this dock with a hand truck and a list, and the foreman signed it over, because you do not refuse the man who kept the light for forty years, not even when he has started keeping it backwards. In the margin: "He counted them out loud. All 219. He said their numbers like names."

notes.location_hint: Works ledger on the catwalk office desk (z_foreman_catwalk)

en.title: Works Order 9-0611 — No Client Line
en.text: A machining order from the stores cage, twelve years before the blackout. Client line: blank. Quantity: four hundred metering drums, special wind. Special instruction, typed: WIND THE SECOND COIL TO PAY CURRENT BACK DOWN THE LINE. The day foreman's stamp across it: REFUSED — A METER MEASURES. Below, in a different ink, the disposition that actually happened: "Reassigned to night shift. The night shift does not read instructions." The shipping stubs stapled behind it name two destinations only — a line through the park, and the hospital sub-feed — and the retired meterman who came asking after his drums three years later was shown the door. His parting line is pencilled on the stub by whoever filed this: "He said, a backwards meter is not a fault, it is a tap, and the substation has never lied to him once."

notes.location_hint: Works-order file in the stores cage (z_stores_yard)

en.title: Switchgear Room — The Winding Refusal
en.text: Clipped inside the switchgear cabinet door, where only the man with the key would ever read it: the winding-room's own refusal, all four engineers' initials, and under it the night foreman's countermand. "We will not wind coils that feed a lamp's memory back into the wire. The order says the lamps will remember. Nobody has said what they will remember, or who is on the other end of the return line, and the council itself denied the program by name — we read it in the paper same as everyone. No." The countermand is one line and it is not angry: "The order stands. Night shift takes it. When you come back in the morning, do not open the drum cage." Below both, the day foreman, last, in the hand that wrote the time cards: "They told us the project was never meant to drink. I have machined things all my life. A thing does what it is shaped to do, and this was shaped thirsty. Every drum that left this dock is drinking somewhere tonight, and I signed the shipping tickets."

notes.location_hint: Clipped inside the switchgear cabinet door (z_switchgear_room)

en.title: Shift Boss's Cassette — Roll Call
en.text: A cassette in the locker-room player, labelled ROLL CALL in grease pencil. The shift boss runs the 22:00 roll the way he has run it for thirty years — Roma. The Zimin twins. Katya's father, who fixed the paint line. He reads each name and pauses for the answer, and the answers come, but they come from the floor, through the wall, spaced like machine cycles — a press-stroke for a yes. He keeps going. He has to reach the end of the list before he can clock anyone out, and no one has ever reached the end. Then, quieter: "The old woman at the pond says you should say their names out loud, and they stand still. She is right. They stand still. Roma stands still. I say his name every night at this bench and for as long as I say it, the press he worked does not cycle. The line took Petrov the same way it took them, and someone is saying his name by the water right now. That is all any of us are now — a name being said by somebody who will not stop."

en.title: Photo: The South Gate, Lit
en.text: Taped to the south gate itself, shot from the catwalk on the first night the plant's own floods held: the gate standing open, the road running south past the works fence toward the substation lights on the far horizon — the center of the web, finally close enough to see from here. The recorder's hand on the back: "Crew log, last entry from this plant. We walked the line in, we will walk it out. The radio voice keeps saying it and it has never once said why — go to the power station, the one who kept the light will meet you at the light. Marat says the voice is a crew we never met. I say the voice knows the lamplighter's order numbers and I heard the man himself count 219 of them at this dock. Whoever meets whoever at that light — the road starts here, and past the substation gate nobody walks back out to tell it. Leave the gate open behind you. It is the last one that swings both ways."

notes.location_hint: Taped to the south gate, shot from the catwalk above (z_south_gate)
